description: Team Dynasty brings together people who have already worked on agricultural projects in Kyrgyzstan and across Central Asia. This experience helped us understand the real decisions farmers face each season, and it shaped Field Shift: a tool built around the needs of farmers and agronomists in the region.
summary:
Farmers in Kyrgyzstan decide what to plant using habit and last year’s prices, while changing climate, water and soil conditions stay invisible from the field. Data that could help exists, but it is scattered: the state knows what grows on each field, and NASA knows the conditions it grows in. In the AgroMap registry, about 45,000 of 108,000 fields list wheat as their last crop, a potential monoculture risk.

We developed a mobile web app that gives every field a “passport.” A farmer taps a field, or uses “My Location” while standing in it, and sees its multi-year crop history, area, soil type and distance to the nearest canal from AgroMap. The passport also shows landslide and debris-flow risk from NASA LHASA and root-zone and surface soil moisture, now and 24 months back, from NASA SMAP L4. Our server extracts only the one ~9 km SMAP cell under the field, so data loads quickly on mobile networks.

This helps farms adapt to changing water, soil and hazard conditions by giving farmers and agronomists field-level evidence for each season’s planning. Because SMAP and LHASA are global, the approach can scale beyond Kyrgyzstan. Next, we plan to add crop-rotation scenarios by income, water and soil.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Shift is a mobile-friendly web map of about 108,000 agricultural fields in Kyrgyzstan. The farmer taps a field, or presses “My Location” while standing in it, and gets a field passport. The passport contains:

  • Multi-year crop history, area, district, soil type and distance to the nearest canal, from AgroMap (the state agricultural registry, via its open GeoServer WFS).
  • Landslide and debris-flow risk from NASA LHASA (global susceptibility map, ~1 km), shown as a map layer and as a risk chip with four classes.
  • Soil moisture from NASA SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP v008): root zone (0–100 cm) and surface (0–5 cm), now and as a 24-month series.

For SMAP, the server finds the granule through NASA CMR and uses OPeNDAP to extract only the single ~9 km cell under the field from the global file. The response is a few kilobytes, so it works on mobile networks. If NASA access fails, the app falls back to an approximation from NASA GIBS.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers and agronomists get field-level evidence for planning each season, instead of relying on habit or last year’s prices. The app also shows monoculture risk (about 45,000 of 108,000 fields list wheat as the last crop), water stress and hazard exposure. Because SMAP and LHASA are global, the approach can be extended to other regions.

Tools and technology

  • Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, beUI components
  • MapLibre GL (WebGL) with PMTiles for fast rendering of ~108,000 field polygons
  • Python scripts (download_agromap.py, build_fields.py, build_web_data.py) to prepare field tiles, passports and the LHASA grid
  • NASA Earthdata (CMR, OPeNDAP, GIBS), Esri World Imagery as basemap
  • Deployed on Vercel

Creativity

We joined two sources that had never been combined at the level of a single field: state field records and NASA satellite data. The server-side extraction of one SMAP cell from a global file keeps the app light, and the “field passport” idea makes complex data readable in one tap.

Factors we considered

  • Mobile first: small payloads and WebGL rendering for farmers using phones in the field.
  • Honest limits: SMAP is a ~9 km cell average, not a sensor in the field, and LHASA is a regional hazard model. We state this in the app.
  • Reliability: a fallback data path if the NASA service is unavailable.
  • Scalability and next step: extend to other regions, and add crop-rotation scenarios by income, water and soil.
dataRefs: NASA SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP v008), NSIDC DAAC
NASA LHASA (Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services), used as a fallback for soil moisture
